findings: Anteroposterior (AP) supine abdominal radiograph including the lower thorax

Radiopaque metallic foreign body in the left upper quadrant overlying the gastric shadow, with the characteristic shape of a small spoon (bowl and handle clearly visible), oriented obliquely with the handle directed inferiorly
Large gas-filled viscus in the left upper quadrant consistent with a distended stomach containing the foreign body
Bilateral renal outlines visible in the mid-abdomen, appearing within normal size limits
Colonic haustral gas pattern visible throughout the abdomen without obvious distension
Lumbar vertebral column visible with no gross osseous destruction seen on this projection
Lower thoracic ribs partially visualised; no definite pneumoperitoneum identified on this supine view
No obvious free intraperitoneal air, though supine projection limits sensitivity for this finding
differential: Ingested intragastric metallic foreign body (spoon) — most likely diagnosis given the classic spoon morphology and location within the gastric gas shadow
Ingested foreign body within the distal oesophagus/gastro-oesophageal junction with gastric distension — less likely given the object appears fully within the stomach
Foreign body within a gastric diverticulum or fundal structure — considered but standard gastric location is most consistent
anatomyConcerns: The spoon is a real radiopaque foreign body and not an anatomical structure; its presence within the stomach carries risk of gastric mucosal injury, pyloric obstruction, or perforation
Supine projection limits detection of free intraperitoneal air; an erect or left lateral decubitus view would improve sensitivity for perforation assessment
The upper thorax and pelvis are not fully included in this field of view, limiting complete survey

imageApproval.diagnosticReason: A clearly defined radiopaque object with the characteristic morphology of a small spoon — a rounded bowl at the superior end and a straight tapering handle directed inferiorly — is visible overlying the gastric gas shadow in the left upper quadrant. The clinical vignette of upper abdominal discomfort after swallowing an object is consistent. No equally supported alternative exists; the spoon shape is distinctive and unambiguous. The stomach bubble is singular and appropriately located. Bilateral renal outlines are present and symmetric. The lumbar spine is midline and continuous. Colonic gas follows a coherent haustra-lined lumen bilaterally. No duplicated organs, floating gas blobs, or impossible anatomy identified. The pelvis is partially visible at the inferior field edge but the groin is excluded. Skeletally mature bony structures consistent with a young adult are present. No lettering or side markers are present.
